summary: How vitamin D, PTH, calcitonin, and FGF23 keep calcium and phosphate in range, how muscle switches fuels as exercise goes on, and which minerals and cofactors bone and muscle depend on. Exam questions pair a lab pattern or an exercise history with the enzyme or hormone step that explains it, such as McArdle disease versus CPT II deficiency.

points: Skin: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3); diet adds D2 and D3
Liver: 25-hydroxylase makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), the main circulating and storage form
Kidney proximal tubule: 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), the active hormone
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D measures status: long half-life (weeks), loosely regulated, reflects skin plus diet supply
Calcitriol has a half-life of hours and is tightly controlled, so it can look normal even in deficiency
1-alpha-hydroxylase is turned up by PTH and low phosphate, and turned down by FGF23 and calcitriol itself
Low ionized calcium is sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid chief cells, which then release PTH
PTH acts on osteoblasts (they carry the PTH receptor), which raise RANKL and lower OPG, so osteoclasts resorb bone
PTH increases calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule and blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Calcitriol raises gut absorption of both calcium and phosphate
Calcitonin from thyroid C cells inhibits osteoclasts; minor role in adult calcium balance
FGF23 from osteocytes rises with high phosphate or calcitriol, causes phosphaturia, and suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Osteoprotegerin (OPG) from osteoblasts is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL and limits osteoclast activation
First seconds: stored ATP plus phosphocreatine; creatine kinase moves phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP
Up to about 2 minutes of hard effort: anaerobic glycolysis of muscle glycogen to lactate
Longer effort: oxidative metabolism of glucose, then a rising share from fatty acid beta-oxidation
Cori cycle: muscle lactate goes to the liver, becomes glucose by gluconeogenesis, and returns to muscle (net cost 4 ATP)
Creatinine forms nonenzymatically from creatine and phosphocreatine at a steady daily rate, so it tracks muscle mass
McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V): autosomal recessive loss of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase)
McArdle: cramps and fatigue in brief intense exercise, myoglobinuria, high CK, blood lactate fails to rise with exercise
McArdle second wind: after about 10 minutes, blood flow brings glucose and fatty acids and the patient can continue
Carnitine shuttle: CPT I on the outer membrane, translocase, CPT II on the inner membrane move long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria
CPT II deficiency: weakness, muscle pain, and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria after prolonged exercise, fasting, cold, or illness
Bone mineral is calcium hydroxyapatite, Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2, laid down on type I collagen
Magnesium is needed for PTH secretion and action; severe hypomagnesemia causes hypocalcemia that persists until magnesium is replaced
Copper is the cofactor for lysyl oxidase, which cross-links collagen and elastin
Vitamin K drives gamma-carboxylation of glutamate on osteocalcin so it can bind calcium in bone matrix
Vitamin C drives prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of collagen (see scurvy)

tricks.label: PTH = Phosphate Trashing Hormone
tricks.text: PTH raises serum calcium but makes the proximal tubule dump phosphate, so serum phosphate falls.

tricks.label: Very Poor Carbohydrate Metabolism
tricks.text: Glycogen storage diseases I, II, III, V: Von Gierke, Pompe, Cori, McArdle. McArdle (type V) is the Muscle one.

tricks.label: 25 for status, 1,25 for action
tricks.text: Order the 25-hydroxyvitamin D level to judge vitamin D stores. Calcitriol is the active hormone but is held steady by PTH, so it misleads.

tricks.label: Sprint versus marathon
tricks.text: Cramps in a short sprint point to glycogen (McArdle). Dark urine after a long run or a missed meal points to fat (CPT II).

highYield: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the best test of vitamin D status
PTH acts on osteoclasts indirectly, through RANKL from osteoblasts
FGF23 lowers phosphate and calcitriol; excess FGF23 causes X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets
McArdle: flat lactate curve with exercise, myoglobinuria, and a second wind
CPT II deficiency: rhabdomyolysis after prolonged exercise or fasting, normal lactate rise
Hypomagnesemia causes hypocalcemia by impairing PTH release and action
Copper deficiency weakens collagen cross-links through lysyl oxidase
Serum creatinine depends on muscle mass as well as GFR
pitfalls: Calcitriol level is a poor marker of vitamin D stores; high PTH can keep it normal while 25-hydroxyvitamin D is low.
Osteoclasts lack the PTH receptor; PTH signals through osteoblasts and RANKL.
McArdle and CPT II both cause myoglobinuria; the trigger (short burst versus prolonged effort or fasting) and the lactate response separate them.
A low serum creatinine in a frail older adult may reflect low muscle mass rather than excellent kidney function.

dumps.p: Draw skin, liver, kidney, gut, bone, and parathyroid. Trace vitamin D from 7-dehydrocholesterol to calcitriol, then add arrows for PTH, calcitonin, FGF23, and OPG with their effects on calcium and phosphate.
l: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol in skin
Liver 25-hydroxylation makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the status marker
Kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylation makes calcitriol
PTH raises RANKL on osteoblasts to activate osteoclasts
PTH increases distal tubule calcium reabsorption and causes phosphaturia
PTH and low phosphate turn on 1-alpha-hydroxylase; FGF23 turns it off
Calcitonin from C cells inhibits osteoclasts
OPG binds RANKL and blocks osteoclast activation

dumps.p: Draw a timeline of exercise from the first second to several hours. Under each phase write the main fuel and enzyme, then mark where McArdle disease and CPT II deficiency each break down.
l: Phosphocreatine and creatine kinase cover the first seconds
Anaerobic glycolysis of glycogen to lactate covers about 10 seconds to 2 minutes
Oxidative metabolism of glucose, then fatty acids, covers longer effort
Cori cycle returns lactate to the liver for gluconeogenesis
McArdle fails early: no glycogen breakdown, no lactate rise, second wind later
CPT II fails late: no long-chain fatty acid entry into mitochondria
Both can cause rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria

summary: The genes that build the skeleton and muscle, and what happens when they fail: transcription factor defects, collagen and dystrophin mutations, repeat expansions, mitochondrial inheritance, and the tumor suppressor and fusion gene changes behind bone sarcomas. Exam questions ask you to predict severity from the type of mutation and to name the inheritance pattern from a pedigree or family history.

points: RUNX2 is the master switch for osteoblast differentiation
RUNX2 haploinsufficiency (autosomal dominant) causes cleidocranial dysplasia: absent or small clavicles, open fontanelles, delayed suture closure, extra teeth
SOX9 drives chondrocyte differentiation from mesenchyme
HOX genes give each body segment its identity along the head to tail axis; mutations put structures in the wrong place (for example HOXD13 synpolydactyly)
Achondroplasia: FGFR3 gain-of-function mutation keeps the receptor active and slows chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate
Endochondral bone is short (limbs) while membranous bone is normal, so the head is large and the trunk near normal
Most achondroplasia cases are new autosomal dominant mutations linked to advanced paternal age
Type I collagen is two alpha-1 chains (COL1A1) and one alpha-2 chain (COL1A2), with glycine at every third residue
Glycine substitution: the bad chain enters many triple helices (3 of 4 when COL1A1 is hit) and spoils them (dominant negative), giving severe OI types II to IV
Null allele: no bad chain is made, only half the normal amount of collagen, giving mild OI type I (blue sclerae, fractures, hearing loss)
DMD gene (Xp21) is the largest human gene, a big target, so about one third of cases are new mutations
Frameshift deletion leads to an early stop codon and no dystrophin: Duchenne, onset by about age 5, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy
In-frame deletion leaves a shorter, partly working dystrophin: Becker, later onset, slower course
Severity follows the reading frame, regardless of deletion size
Dystrophin anchors actin to the dystroglycan complex and extracellular matrix; without it the sarcolemma tears with contraction
Myotonic dystrophy type 1: autosomal dominant CTG expansion in the DMPK gene, toxic RNA disrupts splicing
Anticipation: the repeat grows each generation; maternal transmission can cause a severe congenital form
Features: myotonia (slow grip release), distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy, cardiac conduction block
Mitochondrial DNA comes only from the mother: all children of an affected mother can be affected, none from an affected father
Heteroplasmy: cells carry a mix of normal and mutant mtDNA, so severity varies widely within a family
Ragged red fibers on modified Gomori trichrome are clumps of abnormal mitochondria under the sarcolemma (MERRF, MELAS)
RB1 (13q14) controls the G1 to S checkpoint; a germline RB1 mutation (hereditary retinoblastoma) raises osteosarcoma risk
Germline TP53 loss (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) causes sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, leukemia, and adrenocortical carcinoma at young ages
Ewing sarcoma: t(11;22) fuses EWSR1 to FLI1, making an abnormal transcription factor

charts.title: Musculoskeletal genetic disorders
rows: Absent clavicles, open fontanelles, extra teeth
Short limbs, large head, normal intelligence
Osteogenesis imperfecta types II to IV
Severe fractures and deformity, perinatal death in type II
Myotonia, cataracts, balding, testicular atrophy, conduction block
Ragged red fibers, lactic acidosis, seizures or stroke-like episodes

charts.title: Bone and soft tissue sarcoma genetics
rows: Germline RB1 loss plus second hit
Holds cells at the G1 to S checkpoint
Retinoblastoma in infancy, bone tumor in adolescence
Arrests the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage
Several early cancers in one family
Fusion protein acts as an abnormal transcription factor
Boy with diaphyseal tumor, onion-skin periosteal reaction

tricks.label: My Tonia, My Testicles, My Toupee, My Cataracts
tricks.text: Myotonic dystrophy: myotonia, testicular atrophy, frontal balding, cataracts. Add the heart: conduction block.

tricks.label: 11 + 22 = 33, Patrick Ewing's jersey number
tricks.text: Ewing sarcoma carries t(11;22), the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion.

tricks.label: Count in threes
tricks.text: Codons are read in threes. A deletion that is a multiple of 3 keeps the frame (Becker). Any other size shifts the frame and ends the protein early (Duchenne).

tricks.label: Three out of four
tricks.text: Each collagen I molecule has two alpha-1 chains. If half the alpha-1 chains are faulty, only 1 in 4 molecules is fully normal, so a bad chain hurts more than a missing one.

highYield: RUNX2 loss: cleidocranial dysplasia with absent clavicles
FGFR3 gain of function: achondroplasia, new mutations with advanced paternal age
OI: a bad collagen chain (dominant negative) is worse than no chain (null allele)
Duchenne versus Becker depends on the reading frame; deletion size does not decide it
Myotonic dystrophy: CTG repeat in DMPK with anticipation
Mitochondrial disease: maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy, ragged red fibers
Germline RB1 mutation raises osteosarcoma risk
Ewing sarcoma: EWSR1-FLI1 fusion from t(11;22)
pitfalls: A large in-frame deletion causes Becker while a single-base deletion can cause Duchenne; judge by the frame.
Mild OI type I comes from too little normal collagen; the severe types come from abnormal collagen that poisons the helix.
Mitochondrial disorders skip transmission through fathers; an affected man's children are unaffected.
Achondroplasia spares membranous bone; the skull vault and face grow, so the head looks large.

dumps.p: Draw a type I collagen triple helix with two alpha-1 chains and one alpha-2 chain. Then draw what happens with a COL1A1 null allele and with a COL1A1 glycine substitution, and label which gives mild and which gives severe OI.
l: Two alpha-1 chains (COL1A1) and one alpha-2 chain (COL1A2)
Glycine every third residue fits the tight center of the helix
Null allele: half as much normal collagen (quantitative defect)
Null allele gives mild type I OI with blue sclerae and hearing loss
Glycine substitution chain enters and distorts most helices
Dominant negative effect leaves only about 1 in 4 molecules normal
Glycine substitutions cause severe types II to IV

dumps.p: Make a table with columns for inheritance pattern, how it passes in a pedigree, and one musculoskeletal example. Fill rows for autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive, repeat expansion with anticipation, and mitochondrial.
l: Autosomal dominant: every generation, both sexes (achondroplasia, cleidocranial dysplasia)
Autosomal recessive: carrier parents, siblings at 1 in 4 risk (SMA, McArdle)
X-linked recessive: affected males, carrier mothers, no father to son spread (Duchenne, Becker)
Anticipation: earlier, more severe disease in later generations (myotonic dystrophy)
Mitochondrial: from mother to all children, never through fathers (MERRF, MELAS)
Heteroplasmy explains variable severity in mitochondrial disease
New mutations are common in achondroplasia and Duchenne

summary: How nerves drive muscle: transmission at the neuromuscular junction, the stretch and tendon reflexes, and how electrolytes change excitability. Exam questions ask you to place a weakness at the nerve, the junction, or the muscle, and to separate myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and botulism by their mechanism.

points: Action potential reaches the terminal and opens presynaptic voltage-gated (P/Q-type) calcium channels
Calcium entry triggers SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25) to fuse vesicles and release acetylcholine
Acetylcholine binds postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, ligand-gated cation channels, producing the end plate potential
The end plate potential normally exceeds threshold by a wide safety margin and fires a muscle action potential
Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending the signal
Botulism: toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, so no acetylcholine release; descending flaccid paralysis with dilated pupils
Lambert-Eaton syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic calcium channels reduce release; often paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer
Lambert-Eaton: proximal limb weakness that improves with repeated effort, low reflexes, dry mouth and other autonomic signs
Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors block them and cause complement damage
Myasthenia gravis: weakness worsens with use and late in the day, ptosis and diplopia, normal reflexes and pupils, thymus abnormalities
Muscle spindles lie in parallel with muscle fibers and sense length and rate of stretch
Ia afferents from spindles excite alpha motor neurons to the same muscle (monosynaptic stretch reflex) and inhibit the antagonist
Gamma motor neurons contract the spindle ends to keep it taut and set its sensitivity
Golgi tendon organs lie in series at the muscle-tendon junction and sense tension
Ib afferents act through inhibitory interneurons to relax the same muscle under high tension
Reflex roots: biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1
Neurogenic (lower motor neuron): fasciculations, atrophy, low reflexes, often distal; CK normal or mildly high
Biopsy in denervation: grouped atrophy; after reinnervation, fiber type grouping
Spinal muscular atrophy: SMN1 deletion, anterior horn cell loss, floppy infant with tongue fasciculations
Myopathic: proximal weakness, high CK, reflexes kept until late
Type II fiber atrophy with normal CK points to disuse or corticosteroids
Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold for sodium channel opening, so nerves fire on their own: tetany, perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm
Chvostek sign: tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear twitches the face
Trousseau sign: a blood pressure cuff inflated above systolic for 3 minutes causes carpal spasm
Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the membrane, so threshold is harder to reach: weakness and cramps
Hyperkalemia depolarizes the membrane and inactivates sodium channels: weakness and cardiac arrhythmias

rows: Eyelids and eye muscles, then bulbar
Home canned food, wounds, honey in infants

charts.title: Muscle spindle versus Golgi tendon organ
rows: In series at the muscle-tendon junction

tricks.label: S1, 2 buckle my shoe; L3, 4 kick the door; C5, 6 pick up sticks; C7, 8 lay them straight
tricks.text: Achilles S1 to S2, patellar L3 to L4, biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7 to C8. The main roots to name are S1, L4, C5 to C6, and C7.

tricks.label: Lambert-Eaton gets Easier with effort
tricks.text: Repeated firing lets calcium build up in the terminal, so more acetylcholine is released and strength rises. In myasthenia the receptors are few, so strength falls.

tricks.label: Calcium guards the gate
tricks.text: Calcium on the outside of the membrane stabilizes sodium channels. Take calcium away and the gate opens too easily, giving tetany.

highYield: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release
Lambert-Eaton: anti-calcium channel antibodies, small cell lung cancer, improves with use
Myasthenia gravis: anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, ptosis and diplopia, worsens with use
Ia afferents carry spindle stretch; Ib afferents carry tendon organ tension
Grouped atrophy and fiber type grouping mean denervation and reinnervation
Type II fiber atrophy: disuse or corticosteroids
Hypocalcemia: Chvostek and Trousseau signs from increased excitability
Both low and high potassium cause weakness
pitfalls: Ptosis with dilated pupils and descending paralysis is botulism; myasthenia spares the pupils.
Lambert-Eaton has low reflexes that can briefly return after exercise; myasthenia keeps normal reflexes.
Hyperkalemia causes weakness even though it depolarizes the membrane, because inactivated sodium channels cannot fire.
Steroid myopathy shows normal CK and type II atrophy, unlike inflammatory myositis with high CK.

dumps.p: Draw a neuromuscular junction from the motor nerve terminal to the muscle fiber. Label each step of transmission, then mark where botulinum toxin, Lambert-Eaton antibodies, and myasthenia antibodies act.
l: Action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Calcium triggers SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion
Acetylcholine binds postsynaptic nicotinic receptors
End plate potential triggers the muscle action potential
Acetylcholinesterase ends the signal
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins
Lambert-Eaton antibodies block presynaptic calcium channels
Myasthenia antibodies block or destroy acetylcholine receptors

dumps.p: Draw the knee jerk reflex arc. Label the muscle spindle, afferent fiber type, spinal level, motor neurons, and the antagonist pathway. Add a Golgi tendon organ and its pathway in a second color.
l: Tap stretches the quadriceps and its spindles
Ia afferent enters the cord at L4
Monosynaptic excitation of the quadriceps alpha motor neuron
Inhibitory interneuron relaxes the hamstrings
Gamma motor neurons keep the spindle taut
Golgi tendon organ sits in series at the tendon and senses tension
Ib afferent inhibits the same muscle through an interneuron

summary: How the immune system attacks joints, muscle, and connective tissue: autoimmunity in rheumatoid arthritis and the connective tissue diseases, hypersensitivity types, crystal-driven innate inflammation, and arthritis after infection or vaccination. Exam questions match an autoantibody to its disease and a joint picture to its immune mechanism.

points: Genetic risk: HLA-DR4 (shared epitope); environmental risk: smoking
Peptidyl arginine deiminase converts arginine to citrulline; citrullinated peptides break tolerance
CD4 T cells (Th1, Th17) and B cells drive synovitis; anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc of IgG) appear
TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 inflame the synovium and cause systemic symptoms
Pannus (proliferating synovium with inflammatory cells and granulation tissue) erodes cartilage
RANKL from T cells and synovial fibroblasts activates osteoclasts, giving marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia
Symmetric MCP, PIP, and wrist synovitis; DIP joints spared
Morning stiffness over 1 hour that eases with use; fatigue and low-grade fever
Ulnar deviation, swan neck (PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion), boutonniere (PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension)
Rheumatoid nodules: central fibrinoid necrosis ringed by palisading histiocytes
Felty syndrome: rheumatoid arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia with recurrent infections
SLE arthritis is nonerosive; hand deformities can be correctable (Jaccoud arthropathy)
Systemic sclerosis: sclerodactyly, calcinosis, flexion contractures, Raynaud phenomenon
Mixed connective tissue disease: overlap of SLE, scleroderma, and myositis features with high anti-U1 RNP
Type II (antibody against tissue): rheumatic fever polyarthritis from anti-M protein cross-reaction (molecular mimicry)
Type II: Lambert-Eaton, where antibodies made against tumor calcium channels cross-react with nerve terminals
Type III (immune complex): SLE arthritis and nephritis
Type IV (T cell): polymyositis, with CD8 T cells killing muscle fibers
Gout: macrophages take up urate crystals, NLRP3 inflammasome activates caspase-1, which releases IL-1 beta and recruits neutrophils
Septic arthritis: neutrophil proteases and bacterial enzymes destroy articular cartilage within days
Reactive arthritis: HLA-B27 linked sterile arthritis 1 to 4 weeks after enteric or Chlamydia infection
Parvovirus B19 and rubella infection: symmetric small joint arthritis in adults, mostly women, that mimics rheumatoid arthritis
Rubella vaccination: transient arthralgia or arthritis, most often in adult women

charts.title: Autoantibodies in rheumatic disease
rows: Most specific for RA; can precede symptoms
IgM against IgG Fc; also seen in Sjogren syndrome and chronic infection
Tracks disease activity and lupus nephritis
Anti-SSA in pregnancy risks neonatal heart block

charts.title: Rheumatoid arthritis versus osteoarthritis
rows: Symmetric MCP, PIP, wrist; DIP spared
DIP, PIP, hips, knees, first CMC
Marginal erosions, periarticular osteopenia, even joint space loss
Osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, uneven joint space loss

charts.title: Hypersensitivity types in musculoskeletal disease
rows: IgG or IgM against tissue antigens
Rheumatic fever arthritis, Lambert-Eaton, myasthenia gravis

tricks.label: CREST
tricks.text: Limited systemic sclerosis: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Anticentromere antibody.

tricks.label: HLA-B27: PAIR
tricks.text: Psoriatic arthritis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD-associated arthritis, Reactive arthritis.

tricks.label: ACID
tricks.text: Hypersensitivity types I to IV: Anaphylactic, Cytotoxic (antibody), Immune complex, Delayed (T cell).

tricks.label: Swan neck versus boutonniere
tricks.text: Look at the PIP. A swan's neck arches up (PIP hyperextended). A buttonhole lets the PIP poke through bent (PIP flexed).

highYield: Anti-CCP is the most specific test for rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP; osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis involve it
RANKL-driven osteoclasts cause RA bone erosions
Felty syndrome: RA, splenomegaly, neutropenia
Anti-U1 RNP: mixed connective tissue disease
Gout inflammation runs through the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta
Polymyositis is type IV (CD8 T cell) injury
Parvovirus B19 in adults can mimic early rheumatoid arthritis
pitfalls: Rheumatoid factor alone is not specific for RA; anti-CCP is the better confirmatory antibody.
SLE arthritis does not erode bone; erosions point toward RA.
Lambert-Eaton is type II hypersensitivity even though it starts from a tumor, because antibodies attack a tissue antigen.
Reactive arthritis follows infection by weeks and the joint fluid is sterile; septic arthritis has organisms in the joint.

dumps.p: Draw a normal synovial joint and an RA joint side by side. Label the cells, cytokines, and structures that lead from citrullinated peptides to bone erosion.
l: HLA-DR4 presents citrullinated peptides
CD4 T cells activate B cells and macrophages
Anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor are produced
TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 drive synovitis
Pannus grows over and erodes cartilage
RANKL activates osteoclasts at the joint margins
Periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions on radiograph

dumps.p: From memory, make a two-column table matching each autoantibody to its disease: anti-CCP, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith, anti-Scl-70, anticentromere, anti-U1 RNP, anti-Jo-1, anti-SSA, anti-SSB. Add one clinical clue for each.
l: Anti-CCP: rheumatoid arthritis
Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith: SLE
Anti-Scl-70: diffuse systemic sclerosis
Anticentromere: limited systemic sclerosis (CREST)
Anti-U1 RNP: mixed connective tissue disease
Anti-Jo-1: myositis with interstitial lung disease
Anti-SSA and anti-SSB: Sjogren syndrome

summary: The organisms that infect bone, joints, fascia, and muscle, and the virulence factors that let them do it. Exam questions give a setting (sickle cell disease, a nail through a sneaker, a deep dirty wound, a tick bite) and ask for the organism, its lab features, or the toxin behind the damage.

points: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase positive, coagulase positive
Protein A binds the Fc of IgG, blocking opsonization and phagocytosis
Surface adhesins bind collagen, fibronectin, and fibrinogen in bone and joint tissue
Biofilm on hardware and prostheses shields bacteria from antibodies and antibiotics
Most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis; in children it seeds the metaphysis of long bones
Gram-negative diplococci, often inside neutrophils; ferments glucose only
Pili attach to mucosa and change antigens, so immunity does not last and no vaccine exists
IgA protease cleaves mucosal IgA
Disseminated infection in sexually active young adults: tenosynovitis, pustular skin lesions, migratory polyarthralgia
Or a purulent monoarthritis, often the knee; terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency raises risk
C. perfringens: gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming rod in deep, dirty, low-oxygen wounds
Alpha toxin is a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that destroys cell membranes, causing myonecrosis and hemolysis
Gas from bacterial fermentation produces crepitus in gas gangrene
S. pyogenes: beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive
M protein resists phagocytosis and complement; hyaluronidase and streptokinase help spread along fascial planes
Pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens, linking MHC II to T cell receptors outside the peptide groove and causing toxic shock
Spirochete carried by Ixodes ticks in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States
Larvae pick up Borrelia from white-footed mice (the reservoir); nymphs transmit it to people
Transmission usually needs about 36 hours or more of tick attachment
Deer feed adult ticks and keep the tick population going but are not the bacterial reservoir
Late Lyme disease: intermittent or persistent arthritis of large joints, most often the knee
Spreads through blood from the lung to vertebral bodies, most often lower thoracic and upper lumbar (Pott disease)
Caseating granulomas destroy the anterior vertebral body, spread to the disc and next vertebra, and collapse them
Collapse makes an angular kyphosis (gibbus deformity)
Pus can track along the psoas sheath to form a psoas abscess with groin or hip pain

rows: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase and coagulase positive
Protein A, collagen and fibronectin adhesins, biofilm
Gram-negative diplococci; oxidase positive, glucose fermenter

M protein, hyaluronidase, streptokinase, pyrogenic exotoxins
Cord factor, mycolic acid cell wall

tricks.label: FAKE a Key Lyme pie
tricks.text: Lyme disease: Facial nerve palsy, Arthritis, Kardiac block, Erythema migrans.

tricks.label: Mice hold it, deer feed it
tricks.text: White-footed mice are the Borrelia reservoir for tick larvae. Deer feed adult ticks. Nymphs bite people.

tricks.label: Lecithinase eats lecithin
tricks.text: Cell membranes are rich in lecithin (phosphatidylcholine). An enzyme that cuts it destroys muscle and red cell membranes, the core of gas gangrene.

highYield: S. aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis
Protein A binds IgG Fc and blocks opsonization
Salmonella osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease
Pseudomonas after a puncture through a sneaker sole
Pasteurella multocida after cat or dog bites
C. perfringens alpha toxin is a lecithinase (phospholipase C)
Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens
Pott disease: vertebral collapse, gibbus deformity, psoas abscess
pitfalls: Salmonella is the classic association in sickle cell disease, but S. aureus still causes many of those infections.
Gonococcal joint fluid cultures are often negative; culture or test the urethra, cervix, pharynx, and rectum too.
Deer are the host for adult ticks; mice are the Borrelia reservoir.
Gas gangrene toxin destroys membranes; streptococcal superantigens act by overactivating T cells.

dumps.p: Draw the two-year Ixodes tick life cycle. Label each stage, the animal it feeds on, when it picks up or passes on Borrelia, and the stage of Lyme disease that causes knee arthritis.
l: Eggs hatch into uninfected larvae
Larvae feed on white-footed mice and acquire Borrelia
Larvae molt into nymphs that keep the infection
Nymphs bite humans and transmit Borrelia
Transmission usually needs about 36 hours or more of attachment
Adults feed on deer
Late disease months later causes large joint arthritis, often the knee

dumps.p: Make a table listing each setting for bone or joint infection and the organism it points to. Add the Gram stain or morphology for each organism.
l: S. aureus: gram-positive cocci in clusters, most common overall
Salmonella: gram-negative rod, sickle cell disease
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: gram-negative rod, sneaker puncture or injection drug use
Pasteurella multocida: gram-negative coccobacillus, animal bites
S. epidermidis: gram-positive cocci, coagulase negative, prosthetic material
M. tuberculosis: acid-fast rod, vertebrae
N. gonorrhoeae: gram-negative diplococci, sexually active young adults

summary: Rickets, osteomalacia, and scurvy: two problems of mineralizing bone and one of building collagen. Exam questions give a child's skeletal findings or an adult's bone pain with lab values and ask for the deficiency, its mechanism, or the risk factor behind it.

points: Osteoid is made normally but does not mineralize, leaving wide seams of soft osteoid
Cause is usually vitamin D deficiency; phosphate loss (renal wasting) does the same
Before the growth plates close it is rickets (growth plate and bone); after they close it is osteomalacia (bone only)
Low vitamin D lowers gut calcium uptake, PTH rises, PTH wastes phosphate, and low phosphate stalls mineralization

notes.h: Risk factors for vitamin D deficiency
points: Limited sun exposure, high latitude, covering clothing, and darker skin (melanin blocks UVB)
Exclusive breastfeeding without vitamin D supplements (breast milk is low in vitamin D)
Fat malabsorption: celiac disease, Crohn disease, cystic fibrosis, cholestasis, bariatric surgery
Liver disease (less 25-hydroxylation) and chronic kidney disease (less 1-alpha-hydroxylation)
Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, phenobarbital, and carbamazepine speed vitamin D breakdown
Diffuse bone pain and tenderness, proximal muscle weakness, waddling gait, fractures
Looser zones (pseudofractures): thin lucent bands across the cortex at the femoral neck, pubic rami, ribs, and scapula
Labs: calcium low or normal, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase high, PTH high, 25-hydroxyvitamin D low
Craniotabes (soft skull), frontal bossing, delayed fontanelle closure
Rachitic rosary: swelling at the costochondral junctions
Bowed legs (genu varum) once walking, widened wrists, delayed teeth
Radiograph: widened, cupped, frayed metaphyses with a wide growth plate
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets: excess FGF23 wastes phosphate; vitamin D level normal, calcitriol inappropriately low
Vitamin C is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen synthesis
Underhydroxylated chains cannot form stable triple helices and are degraded, leaving weak vessels and scars
Perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, easy bruising, hemarthrosis, poor wound healing
Children: painful subperiosteal hemorrhage, refusal to walk, and leg tenderness
Risks: diets without fruit and vegetables, alcohol use disorder, older adults living alone, very restricted diets

charts.title: Nutritional bone and collagen disorders
rows: Vitamin D deficiency after growth plate closure; renal phosphate loss
Bone pain, proximal weakness, Looser zones
Vitamin D deficiency in a growing child; X-linked hypophosphatemia
Failed mineralization of osteoid and growth plate cartilage
Rachitic rosary, craniotabes, frontal bossing, genu varum, cupped metaphyses
Vitamin C deficiency from poor diet or alcohol use disorder
Failed prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of collagen
Perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor healing

tricks.label: Same disease, different age
tricks.text: If the growth plates are open, failed mineralization is rickets. If they are closed, it is osteomalacia.

tricks.label: Follow the PTH
tricks.text: Low vitamin D, low calcium absorption, high PTH, phosphate dumped in urine. That chain explains why phosphate is low and alkaline phosphatase is high.

tricks.label: C makes the collagen hold
tricks.text: Vitamin C adds the hydroxyl groups that let collagen chains bond into a firm triple helix. Without it, vessels leak and wounds reopen.

highYield: Rickets and osteomalacia: defective mineralization with excess osteoid
Osteomalacia labs: low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Looser zones are pseudofractures of osteomalacia
Rachitic rosary and craniotabes are signs of rickets
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets: FGF23 excess with normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Anticonvulsants, fat malabsorption, and darker skin raise vitamin D deficiency risk
Scurvy: failed prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of collagen
Perifollicular hemorrhage with corkscrew hairs points to scurvy
pitfalls: Osteoporosis has normal labs and normally mineralized bone; osteomalacia has abnormal labs and soft, undermineralized bone.
Calcium can be normal in vitamin D deficiency because high PTH pulls calcium from bone.
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets does not respond to ordinary vitamin D because the problem is phosphate wasting.
Scurvy bleeding comes from weak vessel walls; platelet counts and clotting tests are usually normal.

dumps.p: Draw a flowchart from low vitamin D to soft bone. At each step write which lab rises or falls, then add the bedside findings in a child and in an adult.
l: Low vitamin D lowers gut calcium and phosphate absorption
Low calcium raises PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
PTH keeps calcium low-normal by resorbing bone
PTH wastes phosphate in urine, so phosphate falls
Alkaline phosphatase rises with osteoblast activity
Osteoid stays unmineralized
Child: rachitic rosary, craniotabes, genu varum, cupped metaphyses
Adult: bone pain, proximal weakness, Looser zones

dumps.p: Draw collagen synthesis from the ribosome to the fibril. Mark the step that needs vitamin C and list the scurvy findings that follow when it fails.
l: Pro-alpha chains made on rough ER
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase need vitamin C
Hydroxyproline stabilizes the triple helix
Hydroxylysine allows glycosylation and later cross-links
Unstable helices are degraded, so collagen is weak
Fragile vessels: perifollicular hemorrhage, bleeding gums, hemarthrosis
Poor wound healing and subperiosteal hemorrhage in children

summary: The inflammatory and overuse disorders of joints, tendons, bursae, and muscle: spondyloarthropathies, crystal arthritis, myositis, polymyalgia rheumatica, fibromyalgia, bursitis, and tendinopathy. Exam questions turn on a few sharp clues, such as crystal shape, which joints are involved, whether CK is high, and which HLA type or infection came first.

points: Ankylosing spondylitis: HLA-B27, young men, enthesitis and bilateral sacroiliitis
AS back pain is worse in the morning and with rest, better with exercise; chest expansion and lumbar flexion fall
Syndesmophytes bridge vertebrae into a bamboo spine
AS complications: anterior uveitis, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, restrictive lung disease, fractures of the fused spine
Reactive arthritis: HLA-B27, 1 to 4 weeks after Chlamydia trachomatis or Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter; joint fluid sterile
Reactive arthritis: asymmetric leg arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum
Psoriatic arthritis: DIP involvement, dactylitis (sausage digits), nail pitting, pencil-in-cup deformity; axial disease linked to HLA-B27
Purine breakdown: hypoxanthine to xanthine to uric acid, both steps by xanthine oxidase
Underexcretion causes most gout: kidney disease, thiazide and loop diuretics, alcohol, low-dose aspirin
Overproduction: Lesch-Nyhan (HGPRT deficiency), tumor lysis, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
Acute gout: hot, red first MTP (podagra) after alcohol or a purine-rich meal
Chronic gout: tophi, punched-out erosions with overhanging edges, uric acid kidney stones
Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the knee or wrist, chondrocalcinosis; linked to hyperparathyroidism and hemochromatosis
Dermatomyositis: complement-mediated capillary injury, perifascicular atrophy, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules; screen for internal cancer
Polymyositis: endomysial CD8 T cells invading muscle fibers, no rash
Both: symmetric proximal weakness, high CK, myofiber necrosis; anti-Jo-1 marks interstitial lung disease risk
Polymyalgia rheumatica: adults over 50 with shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, high ESR, normal CK and strength
PMR travels with giant cell arteritis; new headache, jaw claudication, or visual change signals risk of vision loss
Steroid myopathy: proximal weakness with normal CK and type II fiber atrophy without inflammation
Prepatellar bursitis from kneeling; olecranon bursitis from leaning or trauma; subacromial and trochanteric from overuse
Septic bursitis (most often Staphylococcus aureus) follows a skin break, most often prepatellar or olecranon
Tendinopathy (tendinosis): overuse causes collagen disorganization and neovascularization with few inflammatory cells
Lateral epicondylitis: extensor carpi radialis brevis origin; medial epicondylitis: common flexor-pronator origin
Supraspinatus impingement: painful arc from about 60 to 120 degrees of abduction
De Quervain tenosynovitis: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, positive Finkelstein test
Plantar fasciitis: heel pain with first morning steps; fluoroquinolones raise Achilles tendinopathy and rupture risk

notes.h: Fibromyalgia, JIA, and other soft tissue
points: Fibromyalgia: central pain sensitization; widespread pain for at least 3 months, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, mostly women
Fibromyalgia labs are normal: ESR, CRP, and CK
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: arthritis before age 16 lasting at least 6 weeks
Oligoarticular JIA: young girls, ANA positive, silent anterior uveitis; systemic JIA: daily spiking fever and salmon-colored rash
Adhesive capsulitis: capsular inflammation and fibrosis, loss of both active and passive shoulder motion, linked to diabetes
Ganglion cyst: myxoid degeneration near a joint capsule or tendon sheath, often dorsal wrist, no true lining

rows: Enthesitis and sacroiliitis with new bone formation
Inflammatory back pain better with exercise, low chest expansion, bamboo spine
Anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation, restrictive lung disease, spinal fracture
Kneeling, leaning on elbow, overuse, skin break
Inflammation of a synovial-lined bursa; S. aureus if septic
Local swelling and tenderness over the bursa
Widespread pain at least 3 months, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, normal labs
Chronic pain and disability without tissue damage
Men, alcohol, purine-rich food, diuretics, kidney disease
Urate crystals activate NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta
Podagra, needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, tophi
Erosions, uric acid stones, urate nephropathy
Adults; dermatomyositis also in children and with internal cancer
DM: complement injury to capillaries; PM: CD8 T cells
Proximal weakness, high CK; DM rash (heliotrope, Gottron papules)
Inflammation of shoulder and hip girdle bursae and synovium
Girdle pain and stiffness, high ESR, normal CK and strength
Giant cell arteritis with vision loss
HLA-B27; Chlamydia or Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter
Sterile immune arthritis triggered by bacterial antigens
Arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis, enthesitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum
Epicondylitis, painful arc, Finkelstein test, heel pain

rows: Alcohol, diuretics, kidney disease, high cell turnover

rows: Symmetric MCP, PIP, wrist; DIP spared

rows: Not raised by the myopathy itself

Loss of active and passive motion
Firm cyst, often dorsal wrist, no true lining

tricks.label: Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree
tricks.text: Reactive arthritis: conjunctivitis, urethritis, arthritis.

tricks.label: HLA-B27: PAIR
tricks.text: Psoriatic arthritis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD-associated arthritis, Reactive arthritis.

tricks.label: P for Pseudogout
tricks.text: Pseudogout crystals are calcium Pyrophosphate, Positively birefringent, and rhomboid (Parallelogram-like). Gout crystals are the needles.

tricks.label: Weak or just sore?
tricks.text: Weakness with high CK means myositis. Stiffness and pain with normal strength, normal CK, and high ESR means PMR. Pain everywhere with all labs normal means fibromyalgia.

highYield: Ankylosing spondylitis: HLA-B27, sacroiliitis, bamboo spine, uveitis, aortic regurgitation
Gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals; podagra
Pseudogout: rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals; chondrocalcinosis
Dermatomyositis: perifascicular atrophy and association with internal cancer
Polymyositis: endomysial CD8 T cells
PMR: over 50, high ESR, normal CK; watch for giant cell arteritis
Fluoroquinolones raise Achilles tendon rupture risk
Oligoarticular JIA with positive ANA needs eye screening for silent uveitis
pitfalls: AS back pain improves with exercise; mechanical back pain gets worse with activity.
Gout crystals are negatively birefringent; pseudogout crystals are weakly positive. Shape (needle versus rhomboid) helps settle it.
PMR patients feel weak because of pain, but their strength and CK are normal; myositis has true weakness and high CK.
Tendinopathy is mostly degenerative (tendinosis), so inflammatory cells are scarce on histology.
Psoriatic arthritis can appear before the skin rash; DIP disease with nail pitting points to it over RA.

dumps.p: Draw the purine degradation pathway from AMP and GMP to uric acid. Mark the enzyme xanthine oxidase, the HGPRT salvage step, and write the causes of overproduction and underexcretion beside the pathway.
l: AMP to IMP to inosine to hypoxanthine
GMP to guanosine to guanine to xanthine
Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid
HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine and guanine; loss (Lesch-Nyhan) raises uric acid
Overproduction: tumor lysis, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
Underexcretion causes most gout: kidney disease, thiazides, alcohol
Urate crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta

dumps.p: Build a table comparing dermatomyositis, polymyositis, polymyalgia rheumatica, steroid myopathy, and fibromyalgia. Use rows for strength, CK, ESR, biopsy findings, and one extra clue for each.
l: Dermatomyositis: weakness, high CK, perifascicular atrophy, heliotrope rash and Gottron papules
Polymyositis: weakness, high CK, endomysial CD8 T cells
PMR: normal strength and CK, high ESR, giant cell arteritis link
Steroid myopathy: weakness, normal CK, type II fiber atrophy
Fibromyalgia: normal strength and labs, widespread pain, poor sleep
Anti-Jo-1 points to interstitial lung disease in myositis
Dermatomyositis calls for a search for internal cancer
